anf_compare.notes: Translated from the PG 74 Greek; no published English version was used for wording.

bible_refs.note: Lemma; then δουλεύειν ἐν καινότητι πνεύματος καὶ οὐ παλαιότητι γράμματος in Cyril’s hortatory form (δουλεύσωμεν).
Cyril cites “the Psalmist”, but the wording οὐκ … δίκαιος οὐδὲ εἷς is Paul’s form in Romans 3:10, drawn from LXX Psalm 13:3 (Hebrew/English Psalm 14:3; cf. Psalm 53:3). LXX numbering converted.

choices.why: βραβευτής: literally “umpire, arbiter”; with εἰσηγητής (“proposer, author”) rendered “director and author” of sin.
μυσταγωγός: Paul as “the teacher of the mysteries”.

choices.english: someone took a torch and, right at
choices.why: ἐπ’ αὐταῖς at the break agrees with ταῖς τριόδοις at the start of u04-rem-early (δᾷδά τις λαβὼν ἐπ’ αὐταῖς ἔστησε ταῖς τριόδοις, “taking a torch, set it up right at the crossroads”); the main verb ἔστησε is aorist, so the row ends “someone took a torch and, right at…”, not as a command.

pass_a_gloss: …says Paul that [Romans 8:7: the mind (φρόνημα) of the flesh enmity (ἔχθρα) to God; for to the law of God it is not subjected, nor can it]. If the mind of the flesh fights the law, how not stupefied to think through it are moved to activity (ἐνέργεια) the things thus standing against? What then Paul says? As to the dead to sin he converses with those co-buried with Christ through baptism, and as already having been enriched with the deadening (νέκρωσις) of the passions, to whom it would befit to go outside the law, through being released from the passions condemned (καταδεδικασμένων) through the law. So, we still remaining in the mind of the flesh, the passions denounced and named through the law, he says, worked in us; we were also liable (ὑπεύθυνοι) then to the law, since sin still lived in us. [Lemma Romans 7:6: now we were released (κατηργήθημεν) from the law, having died in that wherein we were held]. For we were bound (ἔνοχοι) to the law, he says, sin having subjected us to it; but if we died in what we were held, that is sin, the law too will surely be idle with it; for it was decreed (τεθέσπισται) because of it, to convict (ἐλέγχῃ) the transgressors. Outside the need of the law therefore the deadened to sin; for we became another's, and him let us serve in newness of spirit and not oldness of letter (γράμμα). [Lemma Romans 7:7] Look how wisely he makes the words on the law; he said [Romans 7:5]; the saying would in no way be freed from suspicion (ὑποψία); one would say at once: umpire (βραβευτής) then and introducer (εἰσηγητής) of sin the law? For if true that in us the passions of the flesh work through it, how not thought also genesis (γένεσις) of sin? What then the mystagogue (μυσταγωγός)? Sharp he meets, and denies that father of sin the law, blames rather the human nature as weak and through it suffering being caught in penalties (δίκαι). Thus he says [Romans 7:7]. See the sobriety (νῆψις): he did not say 'I did not have sin except through law', but rather 'I did not know it'. So not pretext (πρόφασις) of sin the law, but rather indicative (παραδεικτικός) of it, making it manifest to those not knowing, not so that having learned they might work it, since even before knowing they surely did; [there was not righteous, not one], per the voice of the psalm-singer; but so that knowing the unjust they might move over to the better. And it seems to me such a thing happened to the more ancient through the commandment (ἐντολή) of Moses. Let be supposed for the argument a broad road (οἶμος) carrying somewhere, and let be scattered in it much rubble (χερμάς) through the middle, let be dug if it seems also pits (βόθροι); then let there be some walking in it in night and darkness, stumbling very often on things lying in between, and indeed being let down into pits unwillingly; the matter being thus, someone taking a torch (δᾷς) upon them…
pass_b_english: …Paul says, “The mind of the flesh is hostility toward God, for it does not submit to the law of God, nor indeed can it” (Romans 8:7).
If the mind of the flesh fights against the law, how is it not senseless to think that things so opposed to the law are stirred into action through it?

What then does Paul say? He speaks to those who have been buried with Christ through baptism (Romans 6:4) as to people who are dead to sin, and as to people already rich in the deadening of the passions. It would be fitting for them to go outside the law, since they have been freed from the passions that the law condemned.

So, he says, while we still remained in the mind of the flesh, the passions that the law denounced and named were at work in us; and at that time we were also answerable to the law, because sin was still alive in us.
“But now we have been released from the law, having died to that in which we were held captive” (Romans 7:6).

We were liable to the law, he says, because sin had made us subject to it. But if we have died to that in which we were held captive, that is, to sin, then the law too will surely cease to act, together with sin; for the law was decreed because of sin, to convict those who transgress.

So those who have been put to death to sin no longer need the law. For we have come to belong to another (Romans 7:4), and let us serve him in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter (Romans 7:6).
“What then shall we say? Is the law sin?” (Romans 7:7).

See how wisely he frames what he says about the law. He had said, “When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which were through the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death” (Romans 7:5).

But that statement would by no means have been free from suspicion. Someone would at once have replied, “Is the law, then, the director and author of sin? For if it is true that the passions of the flesh are at work in us through the law, how could it not be thought the very origin of sin?”

What, then, does the teacher of the mysteries do? He meets the objection sharply. He denies that the law is the father of sin, and instead lays the blame on human nature, as weak and, through the law, falling under penalties.
This is why he says, “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means! Yet I would not have known sin except through the law” (Romans 7:7).
Notice his sober care. He did not say, “I would not have had sin except through the law,” but rather that he would not have known it.

So the law is not the occasion of sin, but rather points it out, making it plain to those who did not know it. It does this not so that, having learned of it, they might commit it, for even before they knew it they were surely committing it anyway, “for there was none righteous, not even one,” as the Psalmist says (Psalm 14:3; Romans 3:10), but so that, knowing what is wrong, they might turn to better things.
It seems to me that something like this happened to the people of old through the commandment of Moses.
For the sake of the argument, let us suppose a broad road leading somewhere. Let many stones be scattered along its middle, and, if you like, let pits be dug in it as well.
Then let there be some who walk along it by night and in darkness, stumbling very often over what lies in the way, and falling into the pits against their will.
With matters standing so, someone took a torch and, right at…

φησὶν ὁ Παῦλος ὅτι "τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς ἔχθρα εἰς Θεόν· τῷ γὰρ νόμῳ "τοῦ Θεοῦ
οὐχ ὑποτάσσεται, οὐδὲ γὰρ δύναται." εἰ δὲ μάχεται τῷ νόμῳ τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς,
πῶς οὐκ ἀπόπληκτον ἐννοεῖν δι' αὐτοῦ κινεῖσθαι πρὸς ἐνέργειαν τὰ οὕτως
ἀνθεστηκότα; τί οὖν ὁ Παῦλός φησιν; ὡς τεθνεῶσι τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ διαλέγεται τοῖς διὰ τοῦ
βαπτίσματος συντεθαμμένοις Χριστῷ, καὶ ὡς ἤδη τὴν τῶν παθῶν νέκρωσιν
πεπλουτηκόσιν, οἷς ἂν πρέποι καὶ τὸ ἔξω δεῖν ἰέναι τοῦ νόμου, διά γε τοῦ ἀπηλλάχθαι
παθῶν τῶν διὰ τοῦ νόμου καταδεδικασμένων. οὐκοῦν ἔτι μενόντων ἡμῶν ἐν τῷ
φρονήματι τῆς σαρκὸς, πάθη τὰ διὰ τοῦ νόμου κατειρημένα τε καὶ ὠνομασμένα, φησὶν,
ἐνηργεῖτο ἐν ἡμῖν· ἦμεν δὲ καὶ ὑπεύθυνοι τὸ τηνικάδε τῷ νόμῳ, ἅτε δὴ καὶ ζώσης ἐν
ἡμῖν τῆς ἁμαρτίας ἔτι.
Νυνὶ δὲ κατηργήθημεν ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου, ἀποθανόντες ἐν ᾧ κατειχόμεθα. Ἔνοχοι
μὲν γὰρ ἦμεν τῷ νόμῳ, φησὶν, ὑποθείσης ἡμᾶς τῆς ἁμαρτίας αὐτῷ· εἰ δὲ ἀπεθάνομεν ἐν
ᾧ κατειχόμεθα, τουτέστι τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, συναπρακτήσει πάντως αὐτῇ καὶ ὁ νόμος·
τεθέσπισται γὰρ δι' αὐτὴν, ἵνα ἐλέγχῃ τοὺς παραβαίνοντας. ἔξω δὴ οὖν τῆς τοῦ νόμου
χρείας οἱ τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ νενεκρωμένοι· γεγόναμεν γὰρ ἑτέρῳ, καὶ αὐτῷ δουλεύσωμεν ἐν
καινότητι πνεύματος καὶ οὐ παλαιότητι γράμματος. Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; ὁ νόμος ἁμαρτία;
Ἄθρει δὴ ὅπως σοφῶς τοὺς ἐπὶ τῷ νόμῳ ποιεῖται λόγους· ἔφη μὲν γὰρ, ὅτι "ὅτε ἦμεν ἐν
τῇ σαρκὶ, τὰ παθήματα τῶν "ἁμαρτιῶν τὰ διὰ τοῦ νόμου ἐνηργεῖτο ἐν τοῖς μέλεσιν
"ἡμῶν εἰς τὸ καρποφορῆσαι τῷ θανάτῳ·" ἀπήλλακτο δ' ἂν οὐδαμῶς ὑποψίας ὁ λόγος·
ἔφη γὰρ ἄν τις πρὸς ταῦτα εὐθύς Βραβευτὴς οὖν ἆρα καὶ εἰσηγητὴς ἁμαρτίας ὁ νόμος; εἰ
γάρ ἐστιν ἀληθὲς ὡς ἐν ἡμῖν ἐνεργεῖται δι' αὐτοῦ τὰ παθήματα τῆς σαρκὸς, πῶς οὐκ ἂν
νοοῖτο καὶ ἁμαρτίας γένεσις; τί οὖν ὁ μυσταγωγός; δριμὺς ὑπαντᾷ, καὶ ἀποφάσκει μὲν
ὅτι πατὴρ ἁμαρτίας ὁ νόμος, αἰτιᾶται δὲ μᾶλλον τὴν ἀνθρώπου φύσιν ὡς ἀσθενῆ καὶ δι'
αὐτοῦ παθοῦσαν τὸ ἐναλῶναι δίκαις· ταύτῃτοί φησι Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; ὁ νόμος ἁμαρτία;
μὴ γένοιτο· ἀλλὰ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ ἔγνων εἰ μὴ διὰ νόμου. ὅρα τὴν νῆψιν· οὐ γὰρ ἔφη
Τὴν ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ εἶχον, εἰ μὴ διὰ νόμου, ἀλλ' ὅτι μὴ ἔγνων μᾶλλον αὐτήν· οὐκοῦν οὐ
πρόφασις ἁμαρτίας ὁ νόμος, παραδεικτικὸς δὲ μᾶλλον αὐτῆς, τοῖς οὐκ εἰδόσιν αὐτὴν
ἐμφανῆ καθιστὰς, οὐχ ἵνα μαθόντες 197 ἐργάσαιντο, εἴ γε καὶ πρὶν εἰδέναι, πάντως που
καὶ ἔδρων· "οὐ γὰρ ἦν δίκαιος, οὐδὲ εἷς," κατὰ τὴν τοῦ ψάλλοντος φωνήν· ἀλλ' ἵνα τὸ
ἀδικοῦν εἰδότες, πρὸς τὰ ἀμείνω μεταχωρήσειαν. καί μοι δοκεῖ γενέσθαι τι τοιοῦτον
τοῖς ἀρχαιοτέροις διὰ τῆς Μωσέως ἐντολῆς. ὑποκείσθω τῷ λόγῳ πλατεῖά τις οἶμος
ἀποκομίζουσά ποι, καὶ διεῤῥίφθω μὲν ἐν αὐτῇ πολλὴ διὰ μέσου χερμὰς, ὀρωρύχθω δὲ εἰ
δοκεῖ καὶ βόθροι· εἶτά τινες ἔστωσαν οἱ ἐν νύκτι καὶ σκότῳ βαδίζοντες ἐν αὐτῇ,
περιπταίοντές τε καὶ μάλα συχνῶς τοῖς διὰ μέσου κειμένοις, καὶ μὴν βόθροις
ἀβουλήτως ἐγκαθιέμενοι· ἔχοντος δὲ ὧδε τοῦ πράγματος, δᾷδά τις λαβὼν ἐπ' αὐταῖς

review_notes: Staged row fixed in place in tr1.json. Every clause checked against frm_u04_open_source.json. (1) οἷς ἂν πρέποι is a potential optative; 'It is fitting' changed to 'It would be fitting' (modality). (2) The row break was mistranslated: ἐπ’ αὐταῖς agrees with ταῖς τριόδοις, the first words of u04-rem-early (δᾷδά τις λαβὼν ἐπ’ αὐταῖς ἔστησε ταῖς τριόδοις, 'taking a torch, set it up right at the crossroads'), and the verb is aorist, not a command. 'let someone take a torch and, over them…' changed to 'someone took a torch and, right at…', which joins the staged u04-rem-early opening '[…] set it up at the crossroads'. Translator note corrected. The u04-rem-early reviewer (rv3) may want to tidy its opening to read 'the crossroads, and set it up there' so the join is smooth; this review did not touch tr2.json. Scripture: Romans 8:7, 6:4, 7:6, 7:4, 7:7, 7:5 correct; 'the Psalmist' with οὐ … δίκαιος οὐδὲ εἷς is Romans 3:10's form of LXX Psalm 13:3 (English Psalm 14:3), numbering already converted. Negation in Romans 7:7 and 'not the occasion of sin … but points it out' kept exactly.
Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf).

The row opens mid-sentence: φησὶν ὁ Παῦλος completes ὡς αὐτός που from the end of u03-rem-close, so the English opens with an ellipsis. It ends mid-sentence at δᾷδά τις λαβὼν ἐπ’ αὐταῖς; the image continues in u04-rem-early.
βραβευτής: literally “umpire, arbiter”; with εἰσηγητής (“proposer, author”) rendered “director and author” of sin.
μυσταγωγός: Paul as “the teacher of the mysteries”.
ἐν καινότητι πνεύματος: Spirit capitalised as the Holy Spirit, matching the rendering of πνεῦμα in u03-rem-close.
Possible echo of Galatians 3:19 (the law added because of transgressions) in τεθέσπισται δι’ αὐτήν, ἵνα ἐλέγχῃ τοὺς παραβαίνοντας; not cited inline because the wording differs.

ἐπ’ αὐταῖς at the break agrees with ταῖς τριόδοις at the start of u04-rem-early (δᾷδά τις λαβὼν ἐπ’ αὐταῖς ἔστησε ταῖς τριόδοις, “taking a torch, set it up right at the crossroads”); the main verb ἔστησε is aorist, so the row ends “someone took a torch and, right at…”, not as a command.
